title: Notation
body_md:
We use $X$, $x$, etc.\ for entities on the space side of a duality and $A$, $a$ etc.\ for entities on the algebra side.
When referring to an object of a general category (or double category), we use $C$, $D$, etc.
The two-element dualising object is denoted by $\mathbbm{2}$ on either side. For example, $\mathbbm{2}^X$ denotes the set (or distributive lattice) of continuous order-preserving maps from a Priestley space $X$ to the Priestley space $\mathbbm{2}$ while $\mathbbm{2}^A$ denotes the set (or Priestley space) of homomorphisms from a distributive lattice $A$ to the distributive lattice $\mathbbm{2}$. A relation $R$ on spaces will be written $xRy$ and its dual $a\mathbbm{2}^R b$. Similarly, $aRb$ for a relation on algebras and $x\mathbbm{2}^R y$ for its dual.

title: Remark
body_md: We will avoid the terminology of `horizontal' and `vertical' arrows as conventions differ between authors \cite{GrandisPare,Shulman}. While we focus on applications of double categories to categories with relations arising from concrete order-enriched categories, it is sometimes convenient for us to use a more abstract language that can be used for double categories in general. We settled on the compromise recorded in Table~\ref{tab:doublecat-conventions}. Identity proarrows are denoted by $\mathrm{Id}_C:C\looparrowright C$ and identity arrows by $\mathrm{id}_C:C\to C$. For arrows $f,g:C\to D$, we write $f\le g$ if $(f,g):\mathrm{Id}_C\to \mathrm{Id}_D$ is a square. For proarrows $R,R': C \looparrowright D$, we write $R\le R'$ if $(\mathrm{id}_C,\mathrm{id}_D):R\looparrowright R'$ is a square.

label: def:drel
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:drel}
For any concretely order-enriched category $\mathcal C$, its \textbf{double category of relations} ${\mathbb R}\mathsf{el}(\mathcal C)$ is the double category given as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathbb C_0$ is the category $\mathcal C$.
\item $\mathbb C_1$ is the category that has as objects (proarrows) $\mathcal C$-relations $R:C\looparrowright D$ and as arrows (squares) pairs of maps $(f:C\to C',g:D\to D')$ in $\mathcal C$
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=1.2em, row sep=1.2em]
  C \ar[r, "f"] \ar[d, "R"'] & C' \ar[d, "R'"] \\
  D \ar[r, "g"'] & D'
\end{tikzcd}
\]
such that $cRd \ \Rightarrow \ f(c)R'g(d)$.
\item A square $(f,g):R\to R'$ with $R:C\looparrowright D$ and $R':C'\looparrowright D'$ is mapped by $\mathrm{dom}:\mathbb C_1\to\mathbb C_0$ to $f:C\to C'$ and by $\mathrm{cod}:\mathbb C_1\to\mathbb C_0$ to $g:D\to D'$.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

label: def:arrow-proarrow-proj
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:arrow-proarrow-proj}
A double category of relations $\mathbb C$ has an \textbf{arrow projection}, obtained by restricting to squares whose proarrows are identities, and a \textbf{proarrow projection}, obtained by restricting to squares whose arrows are identities.

label: def:flat-ultraflat
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:flat-ultraflat}
A double category is \textbf{flat} if every double cell is determined by its boundary \cite[3.2.1]{Grandis2019}. It is \textbf{ultraflat} if it is flat and invertible squares with vertical or horizontal identities are identity squares \cite[3.2.4]{Grandis2019}.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
${\mathbb R}\mathsf{el}(\mathsf{Pri})$ and ${\mathbb R}\mathsf{el}(\mathsf{DL})$ have arrow projections $\mathsf{Pri}$ and $\mathsf{DL}$, respectively, and proarrow projections $\mathsf{Rel}(\mathsf{Pri})$ and $\mathsf{Rel}(\mathsf{DL})$, respectively. 
More generally, ${\mathbb R}\mathsf{el}(\mathcal C)$ is strict and ultraflat: relations compose on the nose, squares are a property of the boundary, and the projections are poset-enriched.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: This point of view also allows us to view order-enriched categories such as $\mathsf{Pri}$ and $\mathsf{Rel}(\mathsf{Pri})$ as particular cases of double categories.

label: def:opposite-double-cat
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:opposite-double-cat}
The \textbf{opposite} $\mathbb C^\mathrm{op}$ of a double category $\mathbb C$ is obtained by reversing arrows and squares, while leaving proarrows unchanged.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Given a double category $\mathbb C_1\rightrightarrows\mathbb C_0$, relational morphisms are objects of $\mathbb C_1$ and functional morphisms are arrows of $\mathbb C_0$. Reversal of arrows in $\mathbb C_0$ forces reversal of squares in $\mathbb C_1$ because $\mathrm{dom},\mathrm{cod}:\mathbb C_1\to\mathbb C_0$ are functors. In particular, comparison cells $(\mathrm{id}_C,\mathrm{id}_D):R\to S$ reverse, so the order on proarrows is reversed, while comparison cells $(f,g):\mathrm{Id}_C\to\mathrm{Id}_D$ do not reverse.

label: rem:op-arrows-proarrows
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:op-arrows-proarrows}
To see in more detail how the dualising functor $\mathbbm{2}^-$ interacts with the $^\mathrm{op}$ of the theorem, consider the following square and its dual:
\[
  \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.2em, row sep=2em]
    A \ar[r, "f"] \ar[d, "R"'] & A' \ar[d, "S"] &
    \makebox[0em]{} &
    \mathbbm{2}^A \ar[d, "\mathbbm{2}^R"'] & \mathbbm{2}^{A'} \ar[l, "\mathbbm{2}^f"', above] \ar[d, "\mathbbm{2}^S"] \\
    B \ar[r, "g"'] & B' &
    \makebox[0em]{} &
    \mathbbm{2}^B & \mathbbm{2}^{B'} \ar[l, "\mathbbm{2}^g"]
  \end{tikzcd}
  \]
Taking $R,S$ to be identities, we see that $f\le g \ \Leftrightarrow \ \mathbbm{2}^f \le \mathbbm{2}^g$ and taking $f,g$ to be identities, we see that $R\le S \ \Leftrightarrow \ \mathbbm{2}^S \le \mathbbm{2}^R$. 
This aligns with what we said earlier: duality reverses the order between relations but not the direction of relations, and reverses the direction of functions but not the order between functions.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
It is interesting to see how condition \eqref{eq:dual-relation} of Section~\ref{sec:why-order-enriched} arises from the more abstract double categorical point of view. Start with the square in ${\mathbb R}\mathsf{el}(\mathsf{Pri})$ on the left-hand side below, where $a,b$ are clopen subsets of $X,Y$, respectively.
  \[
  \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.2em, row sep=2em]
    X \ar[r, "a"] \ar[d, "R"'] & \mathbbm{2} \ar[d, "\mathrm{Id}_\mathbbm{2}"] &
    \makebox[0em]{} &
    \mathbbm{2}^X \ar[d, "\mathbbm{2}^R"'] & \mathbbm{1} \ar[l, "a"', above] \ar[d, "\mathrm{Id}_\mathbbm{1}"] \\
    Y \ar[r, "b"'] & \mathbbm{2} &
    \makebox[0em]{} &
    \mathbbm{2}^Y & \mathbbm{1} \ar[l, "b"]
  \end{tikzcd}
  \]
  The squares being dual means that the two square conditions must be equivalent, that is, 
  $$
  xRy \Rightarrow a(x)\le b(y) \ \ \Longleftrightarrow \ \ a \mathbbm{2}^R b
  $$
  which is equivalent to $R[a] \subseteq b$ as in \eqref{eq:dual-relation}.

label: rem:jonsson-tarski-morphisms
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:jonsson-tarski-morphisms}
The dualities above are weaker on morphisms than classical J\'onsson--Tarski duality: subordination morphisms need not preserve $\Box$ on the nose (they only force $f\Box\le\Box'f$), and dually one allows relational morphisms between $\mathsf{DGF}$s rather than continuous p-morphisms. Restricting on both sides---to Boolean algebra morphisms with $f(\Box a)=\Box'f(a)$, and to continuous p-morphisms---yields the classical duality: under Stone duality, $f\Box=\Box'f$ is equivalent to the dual map being a p-morphism (lax $f\Box\le\Box'f$ matches ``forth''; colax $\Box'f\le f\Box$ matches ``back'').

label: rem:flipped-splitting
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:flipped-splitting}
The reader by now will be curious about swapping the roles of upper and lower Karoubi constructions. That is, the machinery discussed here suggests we could just as well split idempotent $\mathsf{DL}$-relations above identity and idempotent Priestley relations below identity to obtain a dual version of Theorem~\ref{thm:spl-pri-dl}. While this works out formally, it does not yield anything interesting.

Consider $\mathsf{DL}$-preorders ${\sqsubseteq_A}$ and ${\sqsubseteq_B}$ on distributive lattices $A$ and $B$. These, effectively, are an order-theoretic way to encode lattice congruences on $A$ and $B$. Because the category $\mathsf{DL}$ is exact (is closed under quotients), a $\mathsf{DL}$-relation between $A$ and $B$ compatible with ${\sqsubseteq_A}$ and ${\sqsubseteq_B}$ amounts to a $\mathsf{DL}$-relation between the quotients $A/{\sqsubseteq_A}$ and $B/{\sqsubseteq_B}$. This can be used to show that in the double category ${\mathbb S}\mathsf{pl}_\ge({\mathbb R}\mathsf{el}(\mathsf{DL}))$, the proarrow projection is equivalent to $\mathsf{Rel}(\mathsf{DL})$. Also, $\mathsf{DL}$ is reflective in the arrow projection of ${\mathbb S}\mathsf{pl}_\ge({\mathbb R}\mathsf{el}(\mathsf{DL}))$ in essentially the same way that posets form a reflective subcategory of the category of preorders.

On a Priestley space $X$, an idempotent ${\prec}$ below identity (corresponding to a congruence on the dual distributive lattice) determines a closed subspace consisting of the elements satisfying $x\prec x$ (call these reflexive elements). Because a closed subspace of a Priestley space is a Priestley space, we obtain a dual fact about ${\mathbb S}\mathsf{pl}_\le({\mathbb R}\mathsf{el}(\mathsf{Pri}))$: the proarrow projection is equivalent to $\mathsf{Rel}(\mathsf{Pri})$ and the arrow projection has $\mathsf{Pri}$ as a coreflective subcategory.

title: Definition

\label{def:proximity-lattice}
  A \textbf{proximity lattice} $(A,\vee,\wedge, 0,1, \prec)$ is a distributive
  lattice $(A,\vee,\wedge, 0,1)$ with an idempotent $\mathsf{DL}$-relation $\prec$ below identity.
   
  The category $\mathsf{Prox}$ has arrows $f:(A,\prec)\to(A',\prec')$ which are $\mathsf{DL}$-morphisms and preserve the relation, that is, $a\prec b \Rightarrow \ f(a)\prec' f(b)$.
  The category $\mathsf{ProxRel}$ has arrows $R:(A,\prec)\looparrowright(A',\prec')$ such that ${\prec} \mathrel{;} R \mathrel{;} {\prec'} \,=\, R$.
  The double category ${\mathbb P}\mathsf{rox}$ takes the arrows from $\mathsf{Prox}$ and the proarrows from $\mathsf{ProxRel}$. The squares are inherited from the underlying posets.

label: prop:kohaus-to-prox
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:kohaus-to-prox}
  Mapping a compact ordered space $X$ to its proximity lattice defines a contravariant functor $\mathsf{KOHaus} \to \mathsf{Prox}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we verify that $(A, \prec)$ as defined is a proximity lattice. 
  The set $A$ of pairs $(d, u)$ with $d$ a lower open, $u$ an upper open, and $d \cap u = \emptyset$ forms a distributive lattice (with meets and joins built from intersections and unions). 
  The relation $\prec$ is transitive and below the identity (componentwise order), and satisfies the required axioms: if $(d, u) \prec (d', u')$ and $(d', u') \prec (d'', u'')$, then $u \cup d' = X$ and $u' \cup d'' = X$, which implies $u \cup d'' = X$ (since $u' \subseteq u$ and $d' \subseteq d''$ by the order structure), so $(d, u) \prec (d'', u'')$. 
  To show that $\prec$ is interpolative, suppose $(d,u)\prec(d'',u'')$, ie $u\cup d''=X$.
  Set $K:=X\setminus u$ and $L:=X\setminus d''$. Then $K$ is a closed down-set, $L$ is a closed up-set, and $K\cap L=\emptyset$. 
  By Nachbin separation~\eqref{eq:nachbin-separation}, there exist a lower open $d'$ and an upper open $u'$ with $K\subseteq d'$, $L\subseteq u'$, and $d'\cap u'=\emptyset$. Thus $(d',u')\in A$, and $u\cup d'\supseteq u\cup K=X$ together with $u'\cup d''\supseteq L\cup d''=X$, so $(d,u)\prec(d',u')\prec(d'',u'')$.
  The compatibility with lattice operations follows from the set-theoretic properties of unions and intersections.
  
  On morphisms: For a continuous monotone map $f : X \to Y$ in $\mathsf{KOHaus}$, define $f^* : (A_Y, \prec_Y) \to (A_X, \prec_X)$ by $f^*(d, u) = (f^{-1}(d), f^{-1}(u))$ for $(d, u) \in A_Y$. Since $f$ is continuous and monotone, $f^{-1}(d)$ is a lower open in $X$ and $f^{-1}(u)$ is an upper open in $X$. If $d \cap u = \emptyset$ in $Y$, then $f^{-1}(d) \cap f^{-1}(u) = f^{-1}(d \cap u) = \emptyset$ in $X$, so $f^*(d, u) \in A_X$. The proximity relation is preserved: if $(d, u) \prec_Y (d', u')$, meaning $u \cup d' = Y$, then $f^{-1}(u) \cup f^{-1}(d') = f^{-1}(u \cup d') = f^{-1}(Y) = X$, so $f^*(d, u) \prec_X f^*(d', u')$.

label: rem:proxrel-iso-priestley
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:proxrel-iso-priestley}
Let $X$ be a Priestley space, $A$ its dual distributive lattice (the lattice of clopen downsets), and $A'$ the proximity lattice of the compact ordered space $X$. Then $\phi : A\to A'$ given by $\phi(a)=(a,X\setminus a)$ is an embedding but not an isomorphism in $\mathsf{Prox}$. It does, however, induce a relational isomorphism $A\cong A'$ in $\mathsf{ProxRel}$: writing $aRa'=\phi(a)\prec a'$ and $a'Sa=a'\prec \phi(a)$ for the relations associated with $\phi$, it is not difficult to verify that $R\mathrel{;} S={\le_A}$ (using interpolation of $\prec$) and $S\mathrel{;} R={\prec}$ (using Priestley separation). Thus $A$ and $A'$ are isomorphic as objects of $\mathsf{ProxRel}$ (but not of $\mathsf{Prox}$).

label: def:str-proximity-lattice
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:str-proximity-lattice}
A proximity lattice is \textbf{$\vee$-strong} if it satisfies
$$ x\prec y\vee z \ \Rightarrow \ \exists y'\prec y. \exists z'\prec z.x\prec y'\vee z'$$
and it is \textbf{$\wedge$-strong} if it satisfies
$$ y\wedge z\prec x \ \Rightarrow \ \exists y'\succ y. \exists z'\succ z. y'\wedge z'\prec x.$$
A proximity lattice is \textbf{strong} if it is both $\vee$-strong and $\wedge$-strong.

label: prop:gentzen-cut
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We assume that $A$ is $\vee$-strong, and that $a\prec b\vee c$ and $a\wedge c\prec b$. By $\vee$-strongness there are $b'\prec b$ and $c'\prec c$ with $a\prec b'\vee c'$. Since ${\prec}\subseteq{\le}$ we have $a\le b'\vee c'$, hence by distributivity
  \[
  a \;=\; a\wedge(b'\vee c') \;=\; (a\wedge b')\vee(a\wedge c').
  \]
  Weakening gives $a\wedge b'\prec b$ (from $b'\prec b$) and $a\wedge c'\prec b$ (from $a\wedge c\prec b$ and $c'\prec c$). The join rule for $\prec$ yields $a\prec b$.

label: def:priestley-preorder
title: Definition
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
For a Priestley preorder $(X, \sqsubseteq)$ we have:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item ${\sqsubseteq}$ is weakening: $x \le_X x' \ \wedge \ x' \sqsubseteq y' \ \wedge \ y' \le_X y \ \Rightarrow \ x \sqsubseteq y$
  \item ${\sqsubseteq}$ is closed in the product topology on $X \times X$
  \item ${\sqsubseteq}$ is above the identity: ${\le_X} \, \subseteq \ {\sqsubseteq}$
  \item ${\sqsubseteq}$ is idempotent: ${\sqsubseteq} \mathrel{;} {\sqsubseteq} \,=\, {\sqsubseteq}$
  \end{enumerate}
  To conclude the remark, let us emphasise that $\sqsubseteq$ is indeed a preorder.
head: environment

label: def:quotient-functor
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:quotient-functor}
  The \textbf{quotient} of a Priestley preorder $(X, \sqsubseteq)$ is the quotient space $X/{\equiv}$ equipped with the partial order given by $[x] \leq [y]$ iff $x \sqsubseteq y$. We denote this quotient by $X/{\sqsubseteq}$.
head: environment

label: prop:quotient-to-kohaus
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since ${\sqsubseteq}$ is closed, so is ${\equiv} \,=\, {\sqsubseteq} \cap{\sqsupseteq}$. The quotient of a compact Hausdorff space by a closed equivalence relation is compact Hausdorff.
  The relation $[x]\le[y]\Leftrightarrow x\sqsubseteq y$ is a well-defined partial order on $X/{\equiv}$ (well-defined and transitive by idempotence of ${\sqsubseteq}$; antisymmetric by construction of ${\equiv}$), and it is closed as the image of the closed saturated set ${\sqsubseteq}$ under the quotient map $X\times X\to(X/{\equiv})^2$.
  On morphisms: if $f:(X,\sqsubseteq)\to(Y,\sqsubseteq')$ is continuous, monotone, and preserves ${\sqsubseteq}$, define $X/{\sqsubseteq}\to Y/{\sqsubseteq'}$ by $[x] \mapsto [f(x)]$.

title: Proof
body_md: Assume $a \vee b \in 1R$. By roundness, there exists $c \in 1R$ with $c \prec a \vee b$. title: Proposition

title: Proof
body_md:
Because composition preserves directed joins, Zorn's Lemma yields a maximal pair $(I^*,F^*)$ above $(I,F)$ satisfying $F^* \mathrel{;} I^* \, \subseteq \, \mathord{\le}$. We claim that ${\prec} \, \subseteq \, I^* \mathrel{;} F^*$, so that $(I^*,F^*)$ is an adjoint pair.

  Suppose $c\prec c'$, but towards a contradiction assume that $c \mathrel{(I^* \mathrel{;} F^*)} c'$ fails. In particular, then either $c \mathrel{I^*} 0$ or $1 \mathrel{F^*} c'$ fails.
  By interpolation, pick $c''$ so that $c\prec c''\prec c'$. So
  both $c'' \mathrel{I^*} 0$ and $1 \mathrel{F^*} c''$ fail.
  Now consider the ideal $I^! = I^* \vee \downarrow c''$, and the filter $F^! = F^* \vee \uparrow c''$, both being proper extensions.

  By maximality, $F^* \mathrel{;} I^! \,=\, \mathbbm{2}\times\mathbbm{2} \,=\, F^! \mathrel{;} I^*$.
  That is, there are elements $d$ and $e$ so that $1 \mathrel{F^*} d \mathrel{I^!} 0$ and $1 \mathrel{F^!} e \mathrel{I^*} 0$.
  The joins defining $I^!$ and $F^!$ mean that there are also elements $x$ and $y$ so that $d\prec x\vee c''$, $x \mathrel{I^*} 0$, $c''\wedge y\prec e$ and $1 \mathrel{F^*} y$. But then $1 \mathrel{F^*} d\wedge y$ and $x\vee e \mathrel{I^*} 0$. By Gentzen cut (Proposition~\ref{prop:gentzen-cut}) with cut element $c''$, we have $d\wedge y\prec x\vee e$. So $1 \mathrel{(F^* \mathrel{;} I^*)} 0$, contradicting $F^* \mathrel{;} I^* \, \subseteq \, \mathord{\le}$.

label: prop:box-equiv
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:box-equiv}
$\Box F = \Box F' \ \Leftrightarrow \ F \equiv F'.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\Rightarrow$, assume $\Box F = \Box F'$. We show $F \sqsubseteq F'$ (and $F' \sqsubseteq F$ follows symmetrically). Suppose $a \prec a'$ and $a \in F$. We need $a' \in F'$. Since $a \in F$ and $a \prec a'$, we have $a' \in \Box F$ by definition. But $\Box F = \Box F'$, so $a' \in \Box F' \subseteq F'$.

For $\Leftarrow$, assume $F \equiv F'$. We show $\Box F \subseteq \Box F'$ (and the reverse inclusion follows symmetrically). Suppose $a \in \Box F$, so $a \in F$ and there exists $a' \in F$ with $a' \prec a$. By $F \sqsubseteq F'$, since $a' \prec a$ and $a' \in F$, we have $a \in F'$. It remains to find $b \in F'$ with $b \prec a$. By idempotence of $\prec$, from $a' \prec a$ we obtain $a'' \in A$ with $a' \prec a'' \prec a$. Since $a' \in F$ and $a' \prec a''$, by $F \sqsubseteq F'$ we have $a'' \in F'$. Thus $a'' \in F'$ and $a'' \prec a$, hence $a \in \Box F'$.

title: Proof
body_md: Assume $a \vee b \in \Box F$. Then $a \vee b \in F$ and there exists $c \in F$ with $c \prec a \vee b$. By $\vee$-strongness, there exist $a', b'$ with $a' \prec a$, $b' \prec b$, and $c \prec a' \vee b'$. Since $c \in F$ and $F$ is upward closed, we have $a' \vee b' \in F$. Since $F$ is prime, either $a' \in F$ or $b' \in F$. If $a' \in F$, then $a \in \Box F$. Similarly if $b' \in F$, then $b \in \Box F$.

label: thm:spec-quotient-kohaus
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:spec-quotient-kohaus}
  Let $(A,\prec)$ be a strong proximity lattice and $(\operatorname{Spec}(A),\sqsubseteq)$ the dual Priestley preorder. Then $\operatorname{Spec}(A)/{\sqsubseteq}$ (Definition~\ref{def:quotient-functor}) is a compact ordered space, isomorphic (as an ordered topological space) to $\mathsf{RPFilt}(A)$ (Definition~\ref{def:filt-rfilt-rpfilt}). Moreover, the quotient map $q: \operatorname{Spec}(A) \to \operatorname{Spec}(A)/{\sqsubseteq}$ is continuous and monotone.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We show that the quotient map $q: \operatorname{Spec}(A) \to \operatorname{Spec}(A)/{\sqsubseteq}$ factors through an isomorphism with the space of round prime filters.

  Define $\phi: \operatorname{Spec}(A)/{\sqsubseteq} \to \mathsf{RPFilt}(A)$ by $\phi([F]) = \Box F$. This is well-defined and injective by Proposition~\ref{prop:box-equiv}. It is bijective onto the round prime filters because $\Box F$ is prime (Proposition~\ref{prop:box-prime-strong}) and round (Proposition~\ref{prop:box-is-comonad}), and every round filter equals its roundification (Definition~\ref{def:box-roundification}). 
  We equip $\mathsf{RPFilt}(A)$ with the subbasis $\{G \in \mathsf{RPFilt}(A) \mid a \in G\}$, $a \in A$,  and order $G \le G'$ iff $G \subseteq G'$. 
  
  The composite $\phi \circ q$ is continuous: The inverse image of $\{G \in \mathsf{RPFilt}(A) \mid a \in G\}$ is $\{F \in \operatorname{Spec}(A) \mid a \in \Box F\}$. Since $a \in \Box F$ iff $\exists a' \in F.\, a' \prec a$ and  since $a' \prec a\ \Rightarrow \ a' \le a$, we have
  \[
  \{F \in \operatorname{Spec}(A) \mid a \in \Box F\} = \bigcup_{a' \prec a} \{F \in \operatorname{Spec}(A) \mid a' \in F\}
  \]
  which is a union of basic Priestley opens, hence open. By the universal property of the quotient topology, $\phi$ is continuous.
  
  Define $[F] \sqsubseteq [F']$ in $\operatorname{Spec}(A)/{\sqsubseteq}$ iff $F \sqsubseteq F'$. This makes the quotient $q$ monotone. 
  
  $\phi$ is an order-isomorphism because $[F] \le [F']$ iff $\Box F \subseteq \Box F'$.
  
The space $\operatorname{Spec}(A)/{\sqsubseteq}$ is compact as the continuous image of a compact space. It is Hausdorff because ${\equiv} \,=\, {\sqsubseteq} \cap{\sqsupseteq}$ is a closed equivalence relation (Proposition~\ref{prop:equiv-closed}) on the compact Hausdorff space $\operatorname{Spec}(A)$. The order is closed since $\sqsubseteq$ is closed.
head: environment

label: def:cover-of-kohaus
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:cover-of-kohaus}
The \textbf{cover} of a compact ordered space $X$ is the Priestley preorder $(\operatorname{Spec}(A_X),\sqsubseteq)$ dual to the proximity lattice $(A_X,\prec)$ of $X$ (Definition~\ref{def:kohaus-proximity-lattice}).
head: environment

label: thm:cover-recovers-kohaus
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cover-recovers-kohaus}
Let $X$ be a compact ordered space and $(\operatorname{Spec}(A_X),\sqsubseteq)$ its cover. Then, as ordered topological spaces,
\[
  \operatorname{Spec}(A_X)/{\sqsubseteq} \; \;\cong\; \; \mathsf{RPFilt}(A_X) \; \;\cong\; X^o,
\]
where $\mathsf{RPFilt}(A_X)$ carries the inclusion order of Theorem~\ref{thm:spec-quotient-kohaus}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first isomorphism is Theorem~\ref{thm:spec-quotient-kohaus}, using that $A_X$ is strong (Proposition~\ref{prop:kohaus-prox-strong}). For the second, define $\eta:X\to\mathsf{RPFilt}(A_X)$ by
\[
  \eta(x) \;=\; \bigl\{\,(d,u)\in A_X \mid x\in d\,\bigr\}.
\]
We verify that $\eta(x)$ is a round prime filter, that $\eta$ is a homeomorphism, and that $\eta(x)\subseteq\eta(y)$ if and only if $y\le x$.

\emph{Filter.} The top $1=(X,\emptyset)$ lies in $\eta(x)$. If $(d,u)\le(d',u')$ and $x\in d$, then $x\in d'$. If $x\in d$ and $x\in d'$, then $x\in d\cap d'$, and $(d\cap d',\,u\cup u')$ is a token, so $\eta(x)$ is closed under binary meets.

\emph{Round.} Let $(d,u)\in\eta(x)$, so $x\in d$. The complement $L:=X\setminus d$ is a closed up-set with ${\downarrow} x\cap L=\emptyset$. By Nachbin separation~\eqref{eq:nachbin-separation} there is a token $(d',u')$ with ${\downarrow} x\subseteq d'$, $L\subseteq u'$, and $d'\cap u'=\emptyset$. Then $(d',u')\in\eta(x)$ and $u'\cup d\supseteq L\cup d=X$, so $(d',u')\prec(d,u)$.

\emph{Prime.} If $(d,u)\vee(d',u')=(d\cup d',\,u\cap u')$ lies in $\eta(x)$, then $x\in d\cup d'$, so one of the two tokens lies in $\eta(x)$.

\emph{Continuity.} The preimage of a subbasic open $\{G\mid (d,u)\in G\}$ is $\{x\mid x\in d\}=d$, which is open.

\emph{Order-embedding.} Lower opens are down-sets, so $x\le y$ implies $\eta(y)\subseteq\eta(x)$. Conversely, if $y\not\le x$, then ${\downarrow} x\cap{\uparrow} y=\emptyset$; Nachbin separation~\eqref{eq:nachbin-separation} yields a token $(d,u)$ with $x\in d$ and $y\in u$, hence $(d,u)\in\eta(x)\setminus\eta(y)$. Thus $\eta(x)\subseteq\eta(y)$ if and only if $y\le x$, so $\eta$ is injective and order-reversing.

\emph{Surjectivity.} Let $G$ be a round prime filter of $A_X$, and set
\[
  S \;=\; \bigcap\bigl\{\,X\setminus u \mid \exists d.\;(d,u)\in G\,\bigr\}.
\]
Each $X\setminus u$ is a closed down-set; the family is closed under finite intersections (meets of tokens join the upper components) and contains $X$ (since $1\in G$). Compactness gives $S\neq\emptyset$. Roundness puts $S$ inside every lower open of a token in $G$: if $(d,u)\in G$, choose $(d',u')\in G$ with $(d',u')\prec(d,u)$, whence $S\subseteq X\setminus u'\subseteq d$.
Thus $G\subseteq\eta(x)$ for every $x\in S$.

Moreover, if $S\subseteq d$ for a token $(d,u)$, then $(d,u)\in G$: finitely many of the closed sets $X\setminus u_i$ already miss $X\setminus d$, their meet $(d_*,u_*)$ lies in $G$ and satisfies $(d_*,u_*)\prec(d,u)$, and $G$ is an upset. 
In particular, $S$ is an irreducible closed down-set: if $S\subseteq A\cup B$ for closed down-sets $A,B$ with neither containing $S$, separate ${\uparrow} y$ from $A$ and ${\uparrow} z$ from $B$ for $y\in S\setminus A$ and $z\in S\setminus B$ to obtain tokens $(d,\emptyset)$ and $(d',\emptyset)$ with $S\subseteq d\cup d'$, whence $(d\cup d',\,\emptyset)\in G$ and primeness forces a contradiction. 
Every nonempty closed subset of a compact ordered space has a maximal element \cite[Prop.~VI-5.3]{GierzEtAl}, so irreducibility yields a unique maximal $x\in S$ with $S={\downarrow} x$.
Then $G\subseteq\eta(x)$, and if $x\in d$ then $S\subseteq d$, so $(d,u)\in G$. Thus $\eta(x)=G$.

Since $X$ is compact and $\mathsf{RPFilt}(A_X)$ is Hausdorff, the continuous bijection $\eta$ is a homeomorphism. Combined with the order calculation, $\eta$ exhibits $X^o\cong\mathsf{RPFilt}(A_X)$ as ordered topological spaces.

title: Proof
body_md:
{(1) $\Rightarrow$ (2).} Given an adjoint pair $L \dashv R : (X,\sqsubseteq_X) \to (Y,\sqsubseteq_Y)$, we define $f: X/{\sqsubseteq_X} \to Y/{\sqsubseteq_Y}$ as $f([x]) = [y]$ where $y$ is any element such that $x L y R x$. 
  
  It follows from (Unit) and $\sqsubseteq_X$ being above the identity that such a $y$ exists and from (Counit) that any two such are equivalent. 
  
  Independence of choice of representative follows from monotonicity and the fact that the quotients are partially ordered. 
  
  For monotonicity, if $xLyRx$, $x'Ly'Rx'$ and $x\sqsubseteq_X x'$, then $y\sqsubseteq_Y y'$ because $yRx\sqsubseteq x'Ly'$ implies $y\sqsubseteq y'$, due to (Counit) and weakening with idempotents.
  
  For continuity, note that the lower sets of the quotient $X/{\sqsubseteq_X}$ correspond to subsets of $X$ that are downward closed with respect to $\sqsubseteq_X$; we call these $\sqsubseteq_X$-lower sets. Similarly for upper sets.
  $L^\circ[-]$ (the set-theoretic converse of $L$) sends $\sqsubseteq_Y$-lower sets to $\sqsubseteq_X$-lower sets, and $R[-]$ sends $\sqsubseteq_Y$-upper sets to $\sqsubseteq_X$-upper sets. 
   
  So the inverse image $f^{-1}(D)$ of a $\sqsubseteq_Y$-lower set $D$ is exactly $L^\circ[D]$, and the inverse image of a $\sqsubseteq_Y$-upper set is $R[U]$. Because $X$ and $Y$ are compact and $L^\circ$ and $R$ are closed, $L^\circ[-]$ and $R[-]$ send closed sets to closed sets (as projections of closed sets from compact spaces). So $f^{-1}$ sends closed $\sqsubseteq_Y$-lower/upper sets to closed $\sqsubseteq_X$-lower/upper sets. Since these form a subbasis of closed sets for the KOHaus topology, $f$ is continuous.

  {(2) $\Rightarrow$ (1).} Given a continuous monotone map $f: X/{\sqsubseteq_X} \to Y/{\sqsubseteq_Y}$, we construct an adjoint pair $L \dashv R$.
  \begin{align*}
    x \, L \, y \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad f([x]) \le [y] \text{ in } Y/{\sqsubseteq_Y}\\
    y \, R \, x \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad [y] \le f([x]) \text{ in } Y/{\sqsubseteq_Y}
  \end{align*}
  
  With these definitions, the quotient relations $\bar L$ of $L$ and $\bar R$ of $R$ are weakening relations satisfying $\bar L \dashv \bar R$ (because $\bar L=f_\diamond$ and $\bar R=f^\diamond$), from which it follows that $L$ and $R$ are weakening with respect to the idempotents satisfying $L\dashv R$.

  It remains to show that $L$ and $R$ are closed subsets of $X \times Y$. Let $q_X: X \to X/{\sqsubseteq_X}$ and $q_Y: Y \to Y/{\sqsubseteq_Y}$ be the quotient maps. The order $\le$ on $Y/{\sqsubseteq_Y}$ is closed (since the quotient is a compact ordered space). Now:
  \[
  L = \{(x,y) \in X \times Y \mid f(q_X(x)) \le q_Y(y)\} = (f \circ q_X, q_Y)^{-1}(\le)
  \]
  Since $(f \circ q_X, q_Y): X \times Y \to (Y/{\sqsubseteq_Y})^2$ is continuous, and $\le$ is closed, $L$ is closed. Similarly, $R = (q_Y, f \circ q_X)^{-1}(\le)$ is closed.

title: Proof
body_md: We show that mapping $(X,\sqsubseteq_X)$ to $X/{\sqsubseteq_X}$ as defined above is an equivalence of categories. It is functorial because the identity relation $\sqsubseteq_X$ maps to the identity function on $X/{\sqsubseteq_X}$ and composition of adjoint relations $(L_1 ; L_2 \dashv R_2 ; R_1)$ maps to composition of functions $f_2 \circ f_1$. It is fully faithful by Theorem~\ref{thm:map-kohaus-pri}. It is essentially surjective because every compact ordered space is isomorphic to the quotient of a Priestley preorder (Theorem~\ref{thm:cover-recovers-kohaus}).

label: cor:rel-iso-kohaus
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:rel-iso-kohaus}
  Priestley preorders $(X,\sqsubseteq_X)$ and $(Y,\sqsubseteq_Y)$ are relationally isomorphic if and only if their quotients $X/{\sqsubseteq_X}$ and $Y/{\sqsubseteq_Y}$ are isomorphic in $\mathsf{KOHaus}$.

label: thm:strongification
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:strongification}
  In $\mathsf{Map}({\mathbb S}\mathsf{pl}_\le({\mathbb R}\mathsf{el}(\mathsf{DL})))$, every proximity lattice is naturally isomorphic to a strong proximity lattice.

title: Proof
body_md:
For a proximity lattice $(A,\prec_A)$, 
  define $A^*$ to consist of all pairs $(I,F)$ where $I$ is a round ideal, $F$ is a round filter, and $a\in I$, $b\in F$ implies $a\prec_A b$. 
  $A^*$ is a distributive lattice ordered by inclusion in the ideals and reverse inclusion in the filters. More precisely, if $F$ and $G$ are round filters, then $F\sqcup G$ -- the filter generated by $F\cup G$ -- is round, as is $F\cap G$.
  Likewise, (ideal) joins and intersections of round ideals are round. Thus the lattice operations in $A^*$ are
  \begin{align*}
      (I,F)\wedge (J,G) &= (I\cap J,F\sqcup G)\\
      (I,F)\vee(J,G) &= (I\sqcup J,F\cap G)\\
      \bot_{A^*} &= (\{\bot_A\},A)\\
      \top_{A^*} &= (A,\{\top_A\})
  \end{align*}
Define $\prec_{A^*}$ by $(I,F)\prec_{A^*}(J,G)$ if and only if  $F\cap J\neq\emptyset$.

Evidently, $\prec_{A^*}$ is a distributive lattice weakening relation, and if $(I,F)\prec_{A^*}(J,G)$ then $I\subseteq J$ and $F\supseteq G$. 

To show that $(A^*,\prec_{A^*})$ is join strong, suppose $$(I,F)\prec_{A^*} (J,G)\vee (K,H).$$
Find elements $b\in J$ and $c\in K$ such that $b\vee c \in F$. 
By roundness of $J$ and $K$, find $b',b''\in J$ and $c',c''\in K$ such that $b\prec_A b'\prec_Ab''$ and $c\prec_A c'\prec_A c''$. 
Thus $b''$ witnesses that $(\mathord{\mathrel{\mathpalette\twoheaddownarrow@\relax}} b',\mathord{\mathrel{\mathpalette\twoheaduparrow@\relax}} b') \prec_{A^*} (J,G)$ and $c''$ witnesses that $(\mathord{\mathrel{\mathpalette\twoheaddownarrow@\relax}} c',\mathord{\mathrel{\mathpalette\twoheaduparrow@\relax}} c')\prec_{A^*} (K,H)$. 
Therefore $b\vee c \in F \cap (\mathord{\mathrel{\mathpalette\twoheaddownarrow@\relax}} b' \sqcup \mathord{\mathrel{\mathpalette\twoheaddownarrow@\relax}} c')$,
which is exactly $(I,F) \prec_{A^*} (\mathord{\mathrel{\mathpalette\twoheaddownarrow@\relax}} b',\mathord{\mathrel{\mathpalette\twoheaduparrow@\relax}} b')\vee (\mathord{\mathrel{\mathpalette\twoheaddownarrow@\relax}} c',\mathord{\mathrel{\mathpalette\twoheaduparrow@\relax}} c')$.
This is $\vee$-strongness: interpolants below $(J,G)$ and $(K,H)$ with $(I,F)$ below their join. Dually, $\prec_{A^*}$ is also meet strong.
     
Now define distributive lattice weakening relations ${\Vdash}\colon A\looparrowright A^*$ and ${\Vdash'}\colon A^*\looparrowright A$ by suitable restrictions of membership: $a\Vdash (I,F)$ if and only if $a\in I$ and $(I,F)\Vdash' a$ if and only if $F\ni a$. 
Roundness of $I$ and $F$ ensures that these are compatible with $\prec_A$ and $\prec_{A^*}$. The relations are adjoint, ${\Vdash}\dashv{\Vdash'}$: 
(Unit) If $a\prec_A b$, by interpolation find $c$ in between. Then $a\Vdash (\mathord{\mathrel{\mathpalette\twoheaddownarrow@\relax}} c,\mathord{\mathrel{\mathpalette\twoheaduparrow@\relax}} c)\Vdash' b$.
(Counit) If $(I,F)\Vdash' c\Vdash (J,G)$, then by definition $c\in F\cap J$, so $(I,F)\prec_{A^*} (J,G)$.
The adjunction is a relational isomorphism: if $a\Vdash (I,F)\Vdash' b$, then $a\in I$ and $b\in F$ implies $a\prec_A b$, so ${\prec_A}={\Vdash}\mathrel{;}{\Vdash'}$; and if $(I,F)\prec_{A^*} (J,G)$, then for $c\in F\cap J$ we have $(I,F)\Vdash' c\Vdash (J,G)$, so ${\prec_{A^*}}={\Vdash'}\mathrel{;}{\Vdash}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let ${\Vdash}\colon A\looparrowright A^*$ and ${\Vdash'}\colon A^*\looparrowright A$ be the relational isomorphism of Theorem~\ref{thm:strongification}.
For a round filter $F$ in $A$ define
\[
  \Vdash(F) \;=\; \bigl\{(I,G)\in A^*\ \mid\ \exists a\in F.\, a\Vdash(I,G)\bigr\},
\]
and for a round filter $\mathcal{F}$ in $A^*$ define
\[
  \Vdash'(\mathcal{F}) \;=\; \bigl\{a\in A\ \mid\ \exists (I,G)\in \mathcal{F}.\, (I,G)\Vdash' a\bigr\}.
\]
These maps send round filters to round filters, and their compositions are identities because ${\Vdash}\dashv{\Vdash'}$ is a relational isomorphism.
The dual claim for round ideals is symmetric.
